advances: Coverage of a fixed actual fiber and its local Clarke gradients. This describes possible stationarity features, not a depth certificate for every normal.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
The value is locally Lipschitz since varying the coefficients changes all margins uniformly over the compact fiber by at most a constant times the parameter change. Use 828211a20fa24681 for the attained minimax identity and zero-level conditions. Write $\phi_p(x,\lambda)=\sum_i\lambda_i L_i(z,x)$. For any direction $D$, fix a primal optimizer $x$ at $p$ and let $\lambda_t$ be a dual optimizer at $p+tD$. For $t>0$,
$$
F_z(p+tD)-F_z(p)
\le \phi_{p+tD}(x,\lambda_t)-\phi_p(x,\lambda_t).
$$
Indeed, the first value is the minimum of $\phi_{p+tD}(\,\cdot\,,\lambda_t)$ and $\phi_p(x,\lambda_t)\le F_z(p)$. As $t\downarrow0$, every accumulation point of the compact weights $\lambda_t$ is dual optimal at $p$: the minimum of the weighted margin varies continuously with the parameters and the weights by uniform convergence on $K_z$. Any primal optimizer and any dual optimizer form a saddle pair. Hence at an ordinary differentiability point the directional pairing of the gradient is bounded above, in every direction, by the support function of the compact saddle feature image. Separation puts that gradient in the convex hull of this image. Carathéodory bounds the number of features needed by one plus the parameter dimension. As a differentiability point tends to $p$, choose these representations, pass to convergent subsequences of coefficients, points and weights, and use the same closedness of the primal and dual optimizer graphs. Thus each limiting gradient lies in the convex hull at $p$. Convexification gives the assertion for all Clarke gradients, with the contact and outward-normal conditions from 828211a20fa24681.

For nonfactorization take one fiber $[0,1]\times[-1,1]$ with coordinates $(x,y)$ and two identical margins $L_1=L_2=x$. The value is zero. Nearby margins $(x+\epsilon y+2\epsilon,x)$ have the first margin strictly dominating and a unique minimizing corner $(0,-1)$; the value is smooth in a neighborhood of each such parameter and its gradient is the feature of that corner in block one. Nearby margins $(x,x-\epsilon y+2\epsilon)$ likewise give the feature of $(0,1)$ in block two. If desired divide the tilted margin by $\sqrt{1+\epsilon^2}$, preserving strict dominance for small $\epsilon>0$. The average of the two limiting gradients gives weights $1/2$ in each block but distinct normalized continuous moments. It therefore cannot come from a single common point.
statement: For a fixed compact full-dimensional polytope $K_z\subset\mathbb R^d$ and margins $L_i(z,x)=a_i\cdot z+u_i\cdot x-b_i$, put $F_z(p)=\min_{x\in K_z}\max_i L_i(z,x)$, where $p$ is the tuple of cap coefficients. Each ambient Clarke generalized gradient of $F_z$ is a finite convex combination of features with block $i$ equal to $\lambda_i(z,x,-1)$, where $(x,\lambda)$ is an actual primal-dual saddle pair for $\min_{x\in K_z}\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_N}\sum_i\lambda_i L_i(z,x)$. If $F_z=0$, all such pairs satisfy $L_i(z,x)\le0$, $\lambda_i L_i(z,x)=0$ for each $i$, and $-\sum_i\lambda_i u_i\in N_{K_z}(x)$, for the outward normal cone. The continuous block moments of a convex combination need not factor through one common $x$.
title: Clarke gradients of the coverage value have finite actual saddle contacts
